title: Enuma Elish, Tablet I: the birth of the gods and Tiamat's army
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.2, Poem of Creation (Enuma elish) (ed. A. C. Heinrich, rev. Z. J. Földi and E. Jiménez), SB I) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: Enuma Elish (the Babylonian Poem of Creation), Tablet I: 162 of 162 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (12 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
Before heaven and earth were named, Apsu and Tiamat mingled their waters and the gods were born. Disturbed by their noise, Apsu plans to destroy them; Ea puts him to sleep and kills him, and in his dwelling Marduk is born. Tiamat, urged on by other gods, creates monsters for battle and gives Qingu the Tablet of Destinies.

Enuma Elish ('When on high'), the Babylonian Poem of Creation, tells how Marduk, god of Babylon, defeated Tiamat, created the ordered world and became king of the gods. It was written on seven tablets and recited in Babylon during the New Year festival. The date of composition is debated (proposals range from the 18th to the 12th century BCE); the surviving copies date from the 9th to the 2nd century BCE and come from Ashur, Nineveh, Kish, Babylon, Sippar, Uruk and other sites. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/2/SB/I) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so (BM.36681, BM.36726, BM.37287, BM.37969). The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 162 of the 162 lines of the eBL edition (100%), from 12 tablets in the British Museum: K.5419.C (Nineveh), BM.45528, BM.36726, BM.36681, 1881,0727.80 (Nineveh), BM.46803, K.13299 (Nineveh), BM.37287, Rm.982 (Nineveh), BM.45571, BM.38024, BM.37969.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; < > sign omitted by the scribe, supplied by the editor; : divider sign written on the tablet; (gloss: ...) a note written by the scribe in small signs or in the margin.

translation.text:
1When on high no word was used for heaven,
2Nor below was firm ground called by name,
3Primeval Apsu was their progenitor,
4Matrix-Tiamat was she who bore them all,
5They were mingling their waters together,
6No lea was packed together, no canebrake matted close.
7When no gods at all had been brought forth,

Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges, ink K.5419.c on the bottom edge. About 14 to 16 lines on the obverse and a few lines along the left side of the reverse, consistent with eBL's 16 obverse lines of Tablet I and one reverse line of Tablet II. On this tablet lines 1-2 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken. Lines 3-7 are complete on this tablet.

translation.text:
8Nor called by names, none destinies ordained,
9Then were gods formed within these two.
10Lahmu and Lahamu were brought forth, were called by name.
11While they matured, while they grew tall,
12Anshar and Kishar were formed, surpassing them,
13Lengthy were they of days, added years to years.
14Anu their firstborn was like unto his forebears,
15Anu, his son, became Anshar’s equal.
16Then Anu begot his own equal, Nudimmud,
17Nudimmud was one to dominate his forebears:
18Profound in wisdom, acute of sense, he was massively strong,
19Far more stalwart than his grandfather Anshar,
20No rival had he among the gods his brethren.
21The divine brethren swarmed about,
22Confounding Tiamat as their uproar grew ever more loud,
23Roiling the vitals of Tiamat,
24Their romping troubled the Heavenly Abode.
25Apsu could not lessen their clamor,
26But Tiamat was silent before them.
27Their actions were noisome to her,

34They took counsel concerning the gods their offspring.
35Apsu made ready to speak,
36Saying to her, Tiamat, in a loud voice,
37“Their behavior is noisome to me!
38“By day I have no rest, at night I do not sleep!
39“I wish to put an end to their behavior, to do away with it!
40“Let silence reign that we may sleep.”
41When Tiamat heard this,
42She grew angry and cried out to her spouse,
43She cried out bitterly, outraged that she stood alone,
44This wicked speech had fallen heavy upon her:
45“What? Shall we put an end to what we created?

translation.text:
80The most capable, the sage of the gods, the Lord was conceived,
81In the midst of Apsu was Marduk born,
82In the midst of holy Apsu was Marduk born!
83Ea his father begot him,
84Damkina his mother was confined with him.
85He suckled at the breasts of goddesses,
86The nursemaid who raised him endowed him well with glories.
87His body was magnificent, fiery his glance,
88He was a hero at birth, he was a mighty one from the beginning!
89When Anu his grandfather saw him
90He was happy, he beamed, his heart was filled with joy.
91He perfected him, so that his divinity was unique,
92He was much greater, he surpassed them in every way.
93His members were fashioned with cunning beyond comprehension,
94Impossible to conceive, too difficult to visualize:
95Fourfold his vision, fourfold his hearing,
96When he moved his lips a fire broke out.
97Formidable his fourfold perception,
98And his eyes, in like manner, saw in every direction.
99He was tallest of the gods, surpassing in form,
100His limbs gigantic, by birthright was he surpassing.
101“Mar-Utu, Mar-Utu,

Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges of two joined pieces, ink Rm 982 and 80-7-19,178 on the left edge. About 20 lines on the obverse; the reverse surface is mostly lost but a narrow strip of signs runs down its left side for most of its height, so eBL's 20 obverse and 22 reverse lines are physically plausible, the reverse ones as fragments only. On this tablet lines 82, 84 are entirely broken, of line 97 only one to three signs survive and lines 80-81, 83, 85-96, 98-101 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). translation.text:
104Fifty glories were heaped upon him.
105Anu formed and made rise the four cardinal winds,
106He put them in his hand, “Let my son play!”
107He fashioned dust, he made a storm bear it up,
108He caused a wave and it roiled Tiamat,
109Tiamat was roiled, churning day and night,
110The gods, finding no rest, bore the brunt of each wind.
111They plotted evil in their hearts,
112They said to Tiamat their mother,
113“When he killed Apsu your husband,
114“You did nothing to save him but sat by, silent.
115“Now he has made four terrible winds,
116“They are roiling your vitals so we cannot sleep.
117“You had no care for Apsu your husband,
118“As for Mummu, who was captured, you remained aloof,
119“Since then you churn back and forth, in a turmoil.
120“As for us, who cannot lie down to rest, you do not love us!

translation.text:
127The gods within her rallied around her,
128They took up wicked plans against the gods their ancestors.
129They rallied around and drew up at Tiamat's side,
130Angry, scheming, never lying down to rest night nor day,
131Eager for battle, rumbling, raging,
132Forming a host, that they might start hostilities.
133Mother Hubur, who can form everything,
134Added countless invincible weapons, gave birth to monster serpents,
135Pointed of fang, with merciless incisors(?),
136She filled their bodies with venom for blood.
137Fierce dragons she clad with glories,
138Gave them glories, made them like gods, (saying)
139“Whoever sees them shall go numb with terror!

140“Let their bodies keep leaping forward and never retreat!”
141She deployed serpents, dragons, and hairy hero-men,
142Lion monsters, lion men, scorpion men,
143Mighty demons, fish men, bull men,
144Bearing unsparing arms, fearless in battle.
145Her commands were absolute, no one opposed them,
146Eleven indeed on this wise she created.
147From among the gods her offspring, who made up her host,
148She raised up Qingu, it was he she made greatest among them.
149Leadership of the forces, command of the host,
150Arming, contact, ordering the attack,
151Chief strategist in warfare,
152(All) she entrusted to him, stationed him at the command post.
153“I have cast a magic spell for you. I make you the greatest in the host of the gods,
154“Kingship of all the gods I put in your power.
